Neonates of the Starry skate (Beringraja stellulata) emerge from their egg cases at a total length of approximately 12 cm [Lb = approximately 12 cm], a size that provides a modest starting point for a species that can ultimately reach considerable dimensions. Field surveys conducted in the northeastern Pacific indicate that newly hatched individuals typically measure within a tight range around this value, being fully formed miniatures of the adults. At the opposite end of the size spectrum, the ultimate total length recorded for this species reaches 86.1 cm [Li = 86.1 cm], representing the maximum size an individual can attain. This asymptotic length was derived from extensive sampling of mature specimens across the species' range, with the largest individuals displaying the full expression of the species' growth potential under favorable environmental conditions.

Sexual maturation in the Starry skate exhibits a clear dimorphism in size at puberty, a pattern common among elasmobranchs. Females attain reproductive maturity upon reaching a total length of 47 cm [Lp = 47 cm], whereas males become reproductively active at a slightly smaller size, with puberty occurring at 46 cm [Lp = 46 cm]. This size-based sexual maturation was assessed through examination of gonadal development in individuals collected during seasonal trawl surveys. The difference of a single centimeter reflects the energetic demands imposed on females by gestation and yolk production, which typically require a larger body frame to accommodate litters. These pubertal lengths correspond to roughly 55 percent of the species' ultimate total length of 86.1 cm [Li = 86.1 cm] for both sexes, indicating that growth does not cease at maturity.

Reproductive output in this species has been estimated based on comparisons with related skates of similar body size. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C], females are capable of producing approximately 65 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 65 offspring per year], a value that aligns with the k-selected life history strategy typical of mesopredatory skates inhabiting cool temperate waters. This maximum reproductive rate, derived from comparisons with congeneric species of comparable dimensions, reflects the low fecundity characteristic of many batoid elasmobranchs, which invest heavily in individual pups through extended gestation.

Embryonic development in the Starry skate proceeds at a deliberate pace, consistent with the slow life history of this family. At the same ambient temperature of 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C], the age at birth, or gestation period, has been determined to be approximately 290 days [ab = approximately 290 days]. This extended intrauterine development allows for the production of relatively large, well-developed pups at parturition, minimizing vulnerability to predation during the earliest life stages. The incubation period was calculated from embryo staging studies conducted in aquaria, where captive females laid fertile egg cases that were held at stable thermal conditions. Such a prolonged gestation stands in contrast to the more rapid development observed in smaller skate species inhabiting warmer waters.

Longevity in Beringraja stellulata is substantial, with a maximum lifespan documented at roughly 12 years [am = roughly 12 years] under natural conditions at 8.9 °C [T = 8.9 °C]. This estimate comes from mark-recapture studies and the analysis of vertebral growth bands, a standard technique for ageing elasmobranchs. In concert with this extended lifespan, the species attains a maximum adult wet body mass of 3500 grams [Wwi = 3500 grams], a value derived from allometric scaling relationships between length and mass. The combination of slow growth, late maturation, low fecundity, and considerable longevity places the Starry skate firmly within the spectrum of slow-living elasmobranchs, where population turnover is modest and recovery from overexploitation is predictably slow.
